This module is housekeeping, and it is the most boring page on this site. Work
through it anyway. It takes about 30 minutes, and it is the difference between
spending the first half hour of Module 1 fighting an installer or actually
writing code.

There is nothing to submit. When you reach the [checklist](#checklist) at the
bottom and every box is ticked, you are ready.

## What you are installing, and why

Two separate things, and people mix them up constantly:

| | What it is |
|:--|:--|
| **R** | The language itself. Does the actual computing. On its own, it is a bare window. |
| **RStudio** | The workbench you sit at to write R. Editor, plots, files, help — all in one place. |

You need both, and you install **R first**. RStudio looks for R when it starts up;
if R is not there yet, RStudio will not find it.

::: {.callout-important}
## If your laptop is managed by your institution
Many hospital and university machines block software installation. Do not spend
an evening fighting it — skip to [Option B: Posit Cloud](#option-b-posit-cloud),
which runs entirely in your browser and needs nothing installed. You can follow
every module that way.
:::

## Option A: install on your own computer

### Step 1 — Install R

Go to the [R Project download page](https://cloud.r-project.org) and pick your
system:

- **Windows** — click *Download R for Windows* → *base* → *Download R-x.x.x for Windows*.
  Run the installer and accept the defaults.
- **macOS** — click *Download R for macOS*, then pick the `.pkg` that matches your
  chip. If your Mac is from 2020 or later it is almost certainly **Apple silicon
  (arm64)**; older Intel Macs use the other one. If you install the wrong one R
  will not start, so check: **Apple menu → About This Mac**.
- **Linux** — follow the distribution-specific instructions on that page.

### Step 2 — Install RStudio

Go to the [RStudio Desktop download page](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)
and install the free version for your system. Accept the defaults.

### Step 3 — Open RStudio and find your way around

Open **RStudio** — not R. (On your machine there will be an application called
plain "R" too. You will not use it. If you see a plain white window with a `>`
and nothing else, you opened the wrong one.)

You will see four panes. Only two matter today:

| Pane | Where | What it is for |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Console** | bottom-left | Where code *runs*. Type here for one-off, throwaway commands. |
| **Editor** | top-left | Where code is *saved*. Write your script here. This is the one that matters. |
| Environment | top-right | Lists the objects you have created. |
| Files / Plots / Help | bottom-right | File browser, your plots, and documentation. |

::: {.callout-tip}
## The one habit worth forming now
Write code in the **Editor**, not the Console. Then run the current line with
**Ctrl+Enter** (**Cmd+Enter** on macOS). Code in the Editor can be saved, re-run
and fixed. Code typed into the Console vanishes when you close RStudio, and
nothing is more demoralising than losing a working analysis because it only ever
existed in the Console.
:::

## Option B: Posit Cloud

If installing is blocked, or you just want to start immediately:

1. Go to [posit.cloud](https://posit.cloud) and create a free account.
2. Click **New Project** → **New RStudio Project**.

You now have RStudio in a browser tab. It looks and behaves like the desktop
version, and everything in every module works there. The free tier is generous
enough for this workshop.

The one difference: your files live in the cloud project rather than on your
laptop. To get a data file in, use the **Upload** button in the Files pane
(bottom-right).

## Set up a project folder

R needs to know *where* to look for your data files. The way this goes wrong is
so common that it is worth heading off before it happens.

In RStudio: **File → New Project → New Directory → New Project**. Name it
`r-workshop`, choose somewhere you will find it again (Desktop or Documents), and
click **Create Project**.

Then make two folders inside it. In the Files pane (bottom-right), click
**New Folder** twice and create:

```
r-workshop/
├── r-workshop.Rproj    <- created for you; double-click this to open the project
├── data/               <- the workshop datasets go here
└── output/             <- things you save: plots, cleaned data
```

Why bother? Because opening the project sets R's *working directory* to that
folder. Which means that from then on, this works:

```r
read_csv("data/abcd-synthetic.csv")
```

instead of this:

```r
read_csv("C:/Users/YourName/Desktop/stuff/r workshop v2 FINAL/data/abcd-synthetic.csv")
```

The short version is called a **relative path** — relative to the project folder.
It keeps working when you move the folder, rename your laptop, or send the project
to a colleague. The long one breaks the moment anything changes.

::: {.callout-warning}
## You may see `setwd()` in older tutorials
`setwd("C:/Users/...")` sets the working directory by hand. Avoid it. It hard-codes
a path that exists only on your computer, so the script breaks for everyone else —
including future you on a new laptop. Opening an RStudio Project does the same job
correctly and automatically.
:::

### Get the data

[Download `abcd-synthetic.csv`](../data/abcd-synthetic.csv) and put it in
the `data/` folder you just made.

This is a **synthetic** dataset — generated by a script, containing no real
participant data — but it is deliberately shaped like an ABCD longitudinal
release: one row per participant per visit, with realistic gaps where
measurements are missing.

## Install the packages we use

A **package** is add-on code that someone else wrote and shared. R comes with a
lot built in, but the tools we teach come from packages, so we install them once.

In the **Console** (bottom-left), paste this and press Enter:

```r
install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "readr", "tidyr"))
```

This takes a few minutes and prints a great deal of scrolling text. That is
normal. Some warnings in that output are also normal.

::: {.callout-note}
## You may have heard of "the tidyverse"
These four packages are all part of the **tidyverse**, a family of R packages
that share a common style. You can install all of it at once with
`install.packages("tidyverse")`, and many tutorials do. We install the four we
actually use, and load them one by one, so that you learn *which package each
function comes from* rather than treating it all as one magic blob.
:::

Installing is a **one-time** step. Loading, which you do in every new session, is
a different thing — that is `library()`, and Module 1 covers it.

## Check that it worked

Paste this whole block into the Console. It loads each package and prints what you
have.

```{r}
#| label: verification
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)

cat("R version:  ", R.version.string, "\n")
cat("dplyr:      ", as.character(packageVersion("dplyr")), "\n")
cat("ggplot2:    ", as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")), "\n")
cat("readr:      ", as.character(packageVersion("readr")), "\n")
cat("tidyr:      ", as.character(packageVersion("tidyr")), "\n")

# The |> pipe needs R 4.1 or newer. If this prints 3 numbers, you are set.
c(1, 4, 9) |> sqrt()
```

You should see version numbers and then three numbers. Your versions will not
match these exactly — anything recent is fine.

::: {.callout-important}
## If the last line errored
An error on `c(1, 4, 9) |> sqrt()` means your R is older than 4.1 and does not
have the `|>` pipe, which we use throughout the workshop. Go back to
[Step 1](#step-1-install-r) and install the current version of R. Installing a new
R does not delete the old one, and RStudio will pick up the newer one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## "There is no package called ..."
This means the install did not finish, usually because it was interrupted or the
package name was mistyped. Re-run the `install.packages()` line above and watch
the tail of the output for a line saying which package failed and why.

On Windows, if it asks *"Do you want to install from sources the packages which
need compilation?"*, answer **no**.
:::

## Optional: get a head start

Not required — Module 1 assumes none of it. But if you would like to read ahead:

- [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz) — the standard free textbook for
  exactly the style we teach. Chapters 1–4 overlap with Module 1.
- [Posit's dplyr cheatsheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-transformation.pdf) —
  one page, worth printing and keeping next to you during the live sessions.
- A [past workshop recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7t9JhBJm1pg) on the
  Module 2 material.
